fixes.explanation: False. Isaiah says the scoundrel hatches plots to destroy the poor with lies, “…even when the plea of the needy is just.” Even when. His weapons are destructive, Isaiah says. This is a heavy verse, so I'll just say it plainly: the plea is fair, and he still goes after them.

A silent king would make for a very quiet palace, but Isaiah doesn't say that. His word for how the king reigns is righteousness. Quiet does show up later, though: Isaiah says the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence (verse 17).

Streams of water in a dry land. Isaiah puts it right next to “…the shadow of a great rock in an arid land.” I think water and shade mean the most exactly where there isn't any. Think of how good shade feels after a long stretch in a hot kitchen standing next to the oven.

A royal garden sounds lovely, friend, and I bet it has plenty of water already. But Isaiah puts the streams somewhere else: in a dry land. Same with the great rock, which gives its shadow in an arid land. He's painting these rulers as water and shade in dry places.

Fool is the word. Isaiah says no longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. It comes after Isaiah says a king will reign in righteousness (verse 1). That's a kingdom I'd like to see.

Coward is a decent guess, but it isn't in this verse. Isaiah names the fool and the scoundrel. He says no longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. The word you wanted was fool.
The hungry. Isaiah says the fool “…leaves the hungry empty and deprives the thirsty of drink.” That's a fool who leaves people in need with nothing. Isaiah doesn't soften it, and neither will I.

Worthy it is. Isaiah says the noble man makes honorable plans and “…stands up for worthy causes.” Honorable plans and worthy causes go together in that verse. That's a short sentence with a lot of backbone.
Ripen sounds nice, like a batch coming out right. But Isaiah says the grape harvest will fail, and the fruit harvest will not arrive. Ripening isn't what the verse describes.

A fallen king is a classic reason for mourning, but this passage doesn't mention one. The grief is for “…the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vines…” Isaiah also describes the land of his people as overgrown with thorns and briers (verse 13). The king in this passage is the one who reigns in righteousness (verse 1).

Isaiah says the opposite, friend. He says “…the palace will be forsaken, the busy city abandoned.” That's a palace left behind and a busy city given up. The hill and the watchtower become caves, a delight for wild donkeys and a pasture for flocks.

The wilderness. Isaiah says “Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field.” The wild, empty place gets justice, and the fertile field gets righteousness. Both places get named.
Toil is a good guess if you think righteousness means nonstop sweating. But Isaiah says the work of righteousness will be peace. The service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever.
